The Commonwealth would contribute equity, and Housing Australia would run and oversee the program in states that have referred power or adopted the relevant laws, as well as in the territories. The bill would start the day after it receives Royal Assent, and the accompanying Consequential Provisions Bill would start at the same time but only if this bill also starts.. Low-to-middle-income earners, Housing Australia, and states and territories that participate in the program.

title: Migration and Other Legislation Amendment (Bridging Visas, Serious Offenders and Other Measures) Bill 2023
snippet: passed. Home Affairs. This bill tightens the rules for a group of non-citizens released from detention after a High Court ruling, creating new crimes with fixed minimum penalties for breaking certain visa conditions. It introduces mandatory minimum sentences for holders of a Subclass 070 bridging visa who breach conditions that ban work with children or vulnerable people, approaching schools or childcare centres, or contacting a victim of a violent or sexual offence. The bill also clarifies how authorised officers may fit and use electronic monitoring devices, and sets out when information from those devices can be shared with law enforcement agencies.. Holders of a Subclass 070 (Bridging (Removal Pending)) visa who are affected by the NZYQ High Court decision, particularly those with a history of serious offending.

title: Australian Citizenship Amendment (Citizenship Repudiation) Bill 2023
snippet: passed. Home Affairs. The bill would let a court decide to end a dual citizen's Australian citizenship after a serious criminal conviction. The minister could ask a court to make an order ending citizenship, moving the power from the executive to the judiciary. The bill repeals the provisions the High Court struck down in 2022 and sets up a court-based regime instead.. Dual Australian citizens convicted of serious offences.

title: Fair Work Legislation Amendment (Closing Loopholes No. 2) Bill 2023
snippet: passed. Employment and Workplace Relations. This bill makes further adjustments to the Fair Work Legislation Amendment (Closing Loopholes No. 2) Bill 2023, adding amendments that were not in the original version. The changes alter the start date for several provisions, narrow an exemption from competition law for collective agreements, and replace a regulation-making power with a framework for the Fair Work Commission to handle road transport contractual chains. The bill also introduces a public interest test for registering certain agreements, lets the minister or the commission pause minimum standards orders while they are reviewed, and stops workers from seeking multiple remedies for unfair deactivation or termination.. The changes affect employees, employers, road transport workers and their employers, digital labour platform operators, employee-like workers, and agencies including the Fair Work Commission and the Expert Panel for the road transport industry.

title: Crimes Amendment (Strengthening the Criminal Justice Response to Sexual Violence) Bill 2024
snippet: passed. Attorney-General. This bill would change how sexual violence cases are handled in the criminal justice system. It would add genocide to the list of offences with special protections, remove child-only offences from vulnerable adult complainant rules, and let people 18 or older opt out of child complainant and witness protections. The amendments follow recommendations from an April 2024 Senate committee report and stakeholder feedback.. Vulnerable adult complainants, child complainants and witnesses, unrepresented defendants, and people with non-physical disabilities.

title: National Vocational Education and Training Regulator Amendment (Strengthening Quality and Integrity in Vocational Education and Training No. 1) Bill 2024
snippet: passed. Employment and Workplace Relations. The bill would let the regulator automatically cancel the registration of training providers that have not delivered any training or assessment for 12 consecutive months. Providers could apply for an extension of up to 12 months if they have a reasonable excuse, such as a natural disaster, and extension decisions could be reviewed by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal. The bill would also prevent new providers from changing their approved courses in the first two years, extend the regulator's internal review period from 90 to 120 days, allow the regulator to prioritise applications, let the minister pause new registrations, and strengthen penalties for false or misleading claims..
